extracted.intended_audience: TV viewers and streaming consumers; fans of It's Always Sunny in Philadelphia; readers interested in entertainment controversies
extracted.subtask_description: Explains why specific It's Always Sunny episodes were removed from streaming and the factors platforms use (explicitly or implicitly) to judge and pull controversial TV episodes. Connects the show's case to wider precedents and availability options.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal for blackface/brownface/yellowface
rubrics_metrics.description: An episode is on the banned list because it features an instance of blackface, brownface, or yellowface.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly states that each missing episode was removed for the same reason: the gang’s controversial use of blackface, brownface, or yellowface. Examples given include Dee portraying Martina Martinez in brownface and Mac using blackface to portray a Lethal Weapon character; the text also contextualizes these practices as a "controversial and racist theater practice with a history linked to American minstrel shows."

rubrics_metrics.name: Satire does not guarantee protection from removal
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when offensive imagery is presented satirically or the show condemns characters' actions, platforms may still remove the episodes if they are deemed 'too insensitive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that although the show often condemns the gang's racism ("the show is actually adamantly opposed to the bigotry of its main characters"), Hulu still pulled episodes featuring racist caricatures. It points out that "the satire was clear, but it seems to have been lost" and that streamers may take umbrage with such episodes despite their satirical intent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retroactive reassessment based on contemporary standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Content that aired years earlier can be re-evaluated and removed when judged by modern sensibilities and cultural context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article explains that episodes were removed mid-2020 and that "old TV episodes will be looked at through a 2020s lens," so material "that might have passed as biting satire years ago can be considered highly controversial by today's standards." It also references the speed and decontextualization of the 24-hour news cycle increasing scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Platform-specific distribution and availability decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Streaming platforms, digital retailers, and physical media distributors treat controversial episodes differently; removal from streaming/digital storefronts does not necessarily eliminate physical release.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page documents that Hulu removed episodes, they aren't available to purchase on Apple or Amazon, but the episodes can still be obtained by buying seasons on DVD (if those DVDs are produced). It advises DVDs as an option to see 'banned' episodes and warns about bootlegs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Severity/tone hierarchy in content tolerance
rubrics_metrics.description: Platforms appear more likely to remove overtly racist caricatures (e.g., blackface) than other offensive content (e.g., depictions of homelessness or drug addiction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article suggests networks may find 'obviously distasteful' racist caricatures more objectionable than 'more subtle' offensive themes, noting: 'Perhaps the racist caricatures are more obviously distasteful to Hulu, than something more subtle, like the show's absurd depictions of homelessness or drug addiction.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Precedent from other series informs removal decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes from other satirical comedies have been removed for related reasons and form a body of precedent streaming services may follow.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples cited include South Park (episodes '200' and '201'), Scrubs, 30 Rock, and Community (the latter removed 'Advanced Dungeons and Dragons' for blackface). The piece notes Always Sunny is one episode behind South Park in number removed, linking the show's removals to broader industry trends.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk of misinterpretation mitigates permissiveness for risky satire
rubrics_metrics.description: Because satire can be misread or imitated, creators and platforms face risk when allowing provocative content, increasing the chance of removal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article observes there's 'always a risk that the message will be lost on some viewers, too, and that they may see the humor as something to imitate rather than reflect upon,' implying platforms may act conservatively to avoid such outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Controversial episodes do not necessarily lead to series cancellation
rubrics_metrics.description: A show can sustain controversial content and continue production if factors like timing, continued quality, evolution, and fan support counterbalance calls for cancellation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article lists reasons Why It's Always Sunny escaped cancellation: 'perfect timing, how it consistently remains funny, and how it has evolved,' plus strong fan base and narrative development (e.g., meaningful character arcs). It uses the show's ongoing production (season 18) as evidence that removed episodes don't automatically end a series.
